slot.title: Matched grip and the full stroke
slot.lessonGoal: Hold the sticks in matched grip and play a relaxed full stroke that rebounds to its starting height.
objectives: Hold a drumstick in matched grip, with the fulcrum between the thumb and the index finger
Describe a full stroke: the stick starts high, strikes the head, and rebounds to its starting height
Explain why letting the stick rebound keeps the hands relaxed

visuals.intent: A hand holding a drumstick in matched grip, seen so the fulcrum between the thumb and the index finger is plain, for the Learner to copy.
The four moments of a full stroke in order, raised, striking, rebounding, and back at the starting height, so the Learner sees the stick come back up on its own.

lesson.title: Matched grip and the full stroke
lesson.lessonGoal: Hold the sticks in matched grip and play a relaxed full stroke that rebounds to its starting height.
objectives: Hold a drumstick in matched grip, with the fulcrum between the thumb and the index finger
Describe a full stroke: the stick starts high, strikes the head, and rebounds to its starting height
Explain how letting the stick rebound and keeping the hands relaxed go together

blocks.text: Imagine holding a drumstick in each hand in matched grip: both hands hold their sticks the same way. Keeping your hands relaxed matters because tension can disrupt the flow of the music [1].

In this matched grip, the fulcrum—the point where the stick pivots—is between your thumb and index finger [1]. At the fulcrum, your thumb runs along the stick opposite the first knuckle of your index finger [2]. Your other fingers curl loosely around the stick rather than squeezing it [2].

blocks.caption: A photograph of palm-down matched grip, with the thumb along the stick and the other fingers curled around it.
blocks.alt: A hand holds a drumstick with the palm facing down, the thumb running along the stick, and the other fingers curled around it.

descriptor.caption: A hand holds a drumstick with the palm down, the thumb along the stick, and the fingers curved around it.
descriptor.alt: A hand holding a drumstick, palm down. The thumb points along the stick, while the index finger and remaining fingers curve around it.

sections.heading: A full stroke starts and finishes high

blocks.text: Starting with the stick raised, you send it down to strike the drum, then let it bounce back to where it started [3][2]. This is a full stroke: one hit that begins and ends at the same height [2][4]. The full stroke moves smoothly down and up, with no stopping point along the way [3].

blocks.caption: The Course’s own schematic shows a full stroke: raised, striking, bouncing up, and back at the starting height.
blocks.alt: Four moments run from left to right above a drum surface. Raised shows the stick high; Striking shows its tip touching the surface; Bouncing up shows it moving upward; Back at starting height shows it as high as it began. Arrows connect the downward and upward movement.

descriptor.caption: The Course’s own schematic shows a full stroke: raised, striking, bouncing up, and back at the starting height.
descriptor.alt: Four moments run from left to right above a drum surface. Raised shows the stick high; Striking shows its tip touching the surface; Bouncing up shows it moving upward; Back at starting height shows it as high as it began. Arrows connect the downward and upward movement.

sections.heading: Relaxed does not mean letting go

blocks.text: Your thumb and index finger keep contact with the stick while your fingers and wrist stay relaxed [3]. You allow the drum’s bounce to carry the stick upward rather than holding it back [1]. A full stroke combines a relaxed hold with a return to the starting height [2].

glossary.definition: A way of holding drumsticks with both hands using the same hold.
The support point around which something turns or tilts.
A drum hit in which the stick starts and finishes at the same raised height.
